query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Switching from a high‐thermal-load laser powder bed fusion process to a room‐temperature 3D ink‐extrusion printing followed by a low‐temperature consolidation (sintering) will significantly reduce residual thermal stresses and degradation of mechanical properties in additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-alloyed AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock with particle morphology and size distribution suitable for both conventional LPBF and ink‐extrusion methods.
generation.intervention: Replace the conventional high-energy laser melting process with a room-temperature 3D ink‐extrusion printing method where the powder is dispersed in a suitable binder to form a green part, followed by a low-temperature sintering process to achieve densification.
generation.conditions: Miniature component geometries typical for precision applications; printing performed at ambient temperature; sintering carried out at moderate temperatures (optimized below conventional melting points) to avoid reintroducing high thermal gradients; testing under standard mechanical and microstructural evaluation conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients during printing lead to minimized microstructural defects and lower residual stresses, while controlled low‐temperature sintering preserves phase stability.
generation.mechanism: By eliminating the high local temperatures and rapid cooling rates of LPBF, the ink-extrusion approach avoids the generation of large thermal stresses and phase instabilities. The subsequent low‐temperature sintering step consolidates the material without inducing significant additional thermal stress, resulting in a more homogeneous microstructure and improved mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to components made via conventional high-thermal-load LPBF, the ink-extrusion printed and low-temperature sintered AlCrFeNiSi components will exhibit reduced residual stresses and improved mechanical properties (e.g., enhanced tensile/compressive strength and hardness).
generation.baseline: Conventional LPBF produced miniature components characterized by significant residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity due to rapid solidification.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective for miniature components where the geometry permits full densification at moderate sintering temperatures. Its applicability to larger components or different powder feedstock morphologies may require further adjustments.
generation.uncertainty: Exact sintering temperature and time window for optimal consolidation of AlCrFeNiSi without reintroducing thermal stresses remain to be determined. Furthermore, the scalability of the ink-extrusion method to other geometries is presently uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of miniature components from the identical AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock: one set by conventional LPBF and another by 3D ink‐extrusion printing followed by an optimized low‐temperature sintering process. Evaluate and compare their residual stress levels (using, for example, X‐ray diffraction methods), mechanical properties (hardness, tensile/compressive strength), and microstructural homogeneity via SEM/TEM analysis.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ink‐extrusion printed and sintered components do not show a statistically significant reduction in residual thermal stresses and an improvement in mechanical properties relative to the LPBF components, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract An oxygen‐resistant refractory high‐entropy alloy is synthesized in microlattice or bulk form by 3D ink‐extrusion printing, interdiffusion, and silicide coating. Additive manufacturing of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is implemented by extruding inks containing hydride powders, de‐binding under H 2 , and sintering under vacuum. The sequential decomposition of hydride powders (HfH 2 +NbH+TaH 0.5 +TiH 2 +ZrH 2 ) is followed by in situ X‐ray diffraction. Upon sintering at 1400 °C for 18 h, a nearly fully densified, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy is synthesized; on slow cooling, both α‐HCP and β‐BCC phases are formed, but on quenching, a metastable single β‐BCC phase is obtained. Printed and sintered HfNbTaTiZr alloys with ≈1 wt.% O shows excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures. Oxidation resistance is achieved by silicide coating via pack cementation. A small‐size lattice‐core sandwich is fabricated and tested with high‐temperature flames to demonstrate the versatility of this sequential approach (printing, sintering, and siliconizing) for high‐temperature, high‐stress applications of refractory high‐entropy alloys. Keywords: additive manufacturing, direct ink writing, oxid

Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEA, also called multi‐principal‐element refractory alloys) comprise five or more principal elements from the refractory transition metals (group 4–6 elements: Zr, Hf, V, Nb, Ta, Mo, and W, often with Ti and Cr also considered), [ [1] , [2] , [3] ] with structural applications under extreme temperature conditions, beyond those where nickel‐based superalloys can be used. [ [4] ] Additive manufacturing (AM) of RHEAs can facilitate the exploration of possible applications for RHEA via rapid prototyping of parts with complex shapes with high powder feedstock utilization. Recently, laser melting deposition (LMD) was used to fabricate NbTaTiZr, [ [5] ] HfNbTiZr, [ [6] ] HfNbTaTiZr, [ [7] , [8] ] and MoNbTaW [ [9] , [10] , [11] ] quaternary and quinary refractory concentrated alloys. However, the feature resolution of LMD is relatively low, as the size of the melt pool is as large as ≈3 mm. [ [7] , [8] ] In addition, no complex parts have been demonstrated for these refractory alloys by using LMD. Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.
